newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Car theft becomes Pakistan national racket.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Car theft becomes Pakistan national racket.

text.p: Five gunmen force a new car to a halt on a busy Karachi street, drag out its hapless owner and drive away, barely noticed by passersby.
It is one of dozens of car thefts reported daily in the sprawling southern Pakistani port, whose estimated 12 million residents are plagued by crime and political violence.

"I became almost numb with fear when I saw the pistol pointing towards my head," said the young victim, Faisal Ayaz. "It is one thing to read about car-snatching incidents in newspapers, but personal experience is terrible."
Car theft figures have soared this year. On average more than 1,000 cars and motorcycles are stolen every month in Karachi, making it the city's top reported crime.
This year's comparative lull in political unrest has brought the spotlight back to non-political crime.

"When there was violence in Karachi, people gave little notice to car thefts. But the problem again began to hit the headlines as now there is relative peace," Mohammad Iqbal, deputy inspector general of Karachi police, told Reuters.
EASY MONEY - AND NOT JUST FOR COMMON THIEVES
Police figures show that thieves grabbed more than 5,000 vehicles in the first five months of 1997, compared to 8,153 in the whole of last year and more than 9,600 in 1995.

"It's easy money and several influential people, from tribal chiefs-turned-politicians to government officials, are involved in this dirty business, harbouring car-snatchers and buying and selling stolen cars," Jameel Yousuf, chief of Karachi's Citizen Police Liaison Committee, said.

"It is a big racket and a national problem. New vehicles snatched from Karachi are sold not just in rural parts of Sindh province or Punjab and Baluchistan provinces, but make their way even to neighbouring Afghanistan," he said.
Older stolen cars are cannibalised for spare parts that are sold in car workshops and markets.
Yousuf said recovery of stolen vehicles was difficult because there was no coordination between the provinces.
"The police lack proper data and information about the vehicles snatched from other cities," he said.

"We have suggested setting up a computerised national vehicle registration unit and a theft-and-recoveries authority under the federal government to combat car theft, but it is yet to materialise," Yousuf said.
INSURERS SUFFER
Police say they recover 30 to 35 percent of stolen vehicles, but the figure includes those abandoned by the thieves after being used in some other crime or stripped for spare parts.
The car theft spree has hit insurance firms, with rising demand for vehicle insurance matched by increasing claims.
According to the Pakistan Insurance Association, only 200 to 300 of the 2,000 insured cars stolen in Karachi in 1996 were recovered.
"People get car insurance first and then bring a new vehicle from the car showroom," said Aman Sabir, manager of vehicles recovery at Adamjee Insurance Company.

In many cases, new cars are snatched in the first year of their insurance, he said, adding claims for such thefts were very costly to the company, which has set annual premiums at six percent of the total cost of the vehicle.
"We have become selective in getting new clients because in several cases, owners have made wrongful complaints of car snatching to make claims," Sabir said.
ORDINARY CUSTOMERS BEAR THE BRUNT
Sabir said his company preferred corporate clients and sought a recommendation before accepting an individual client.
"Pakistan has become a big market for stolen cars and even vehicles snatched in Europe are being sold here," he said.
Yousuf said ordinary people were finding it harder to obtain car insurance and were forced to pay high premiums.

Vehicles recovered in other cities were often not returned to their owners for lack of agreed procedures. "Such vehicles are used by government officials under a controversial law which has been repealed in Sindh province," he said.
In most cases, stolen vehicles were legalised by forged documents and resold in some other city, he said.
